intro.text: This is Tamil Nadu, right down at the bottom of India on the east side. The sea runs along one edge of it and high hills run along the other, with Kerala over on the far side of them. At the very bottom the land comes to a point, and three different seas meet there. The main city is Chennai.

animal.text: The Nilgiri tahr is a wild goat. He lives on the cliffs up in these hills and nowhere else on earth, and he climbs rock that you could not even stand on.

food.text: An idli is a little white cake, soft as a pillow. Rice and lentils are ground up, left to sit overnight, and then cooked in steam. You dip it in a soup called sambar.

festival.text: At Pongal, rice is boiled with milk until it froths up and spills over the side of the pot. Everybody wants it to spill. When it does, they all shout Pongalo Pongal.

hello.text: In Tamil Nadu people say Vanakkam. The language is Tamil, and people were already writing it down more than two thousand years ago. They are still writing it now.

line.text: Fourteen towers stand over this temple, and each one is covered from the bottom to the very top with figures: gods, saints and heroes, packed in row on row. Inside is a hall called the Thousand Pillars. Somebody counted them. There are nine hundred and eighty-five.

A rock as tall as a house sits on a bare slope, tipped over, looking as though it is just about to roll. It never has. A long time ago somebody tried to move it out of the way with seven elephants, and it did not move at all.

This little steam train climbs a mountain. Between the two ordinary rails there is a third one with teeth all along it, and a cogwheel underneath bites into those teeth so the train cannot slip back down. The engine rides at the bottom end and pushes.

The railway line runs off the end of the land and keeps going, straight out over two kilometres of open sea, to an island. When a tall ship needs to get past, a whole piece of the middle of the bridge lifts straight up into the air to let it through.

These trees stand in the water all the time and never come out of it. They hold themselves up on roots like stilts, and between them are little islands and narrow green channels. Herons and pelicans come here to fish.
